name: ZeroSearch: Incentivize the Search Capability of LLMs without Searching
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2505.04588, cs.CL); submitted 7 May 2025, v3 revised 19 May 2026. The authors' own BibTeX cites it as an arXiv article (year=2025). NeurIPS 2025 acceptance could NOT be verified: the OpenReview record shows the paper as an ICLR 2026 Conference Desk Rejected Submission (id mmkbgNlrJB) plus a CoRR 2025 version, and the GitHub/homepage list no peer-reviewed venue. The 'NeurIPS 2025' label in the task metadata is therefore treated as [uncertain].
authors_affiliation: Hao Sun, Zile Qiao, Jiayan Guo, Xuanbo Fan, Yingyan Hou, Yong Jiang, Pengjun Xie, Yan Zhang, Fei Huang, Jingren Zhou. Affiliation: Tongyi Lab, Alibaba Group (lead author Hao Sun also affiliated with Peking University, per contact email sunhao@stu.pku.edu.cn). Corresponding authors: Jiayan Guo and Yan Zhang.
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/ZeroSearch (Apache-2.0; ~1254 stars; homepage https://alibaba-nlp.github.io/ZeroSearch; models/datasets on Hugging Face under sunhaonlp/Alibaba-NLP, e.g. https://huggingface.co/datasets/sunhaonlp/ZeroSearch_dataset)
task_domain: QA (open-domain single-hop and multi-hop question answering); RL-trained agentic search / retrieval-augmented reasoning. The core contribution is a training methodology (search-engine simulation for RL) rather than a new task.
problem_setting: Interactive, multi-turn, single-agent setting where an LLM policy model is trained with reinforcement learning to interleave reasoning (<think>), search queries (<search>), and answers (<answer>). The key problem: prior RL-for-search methods (e.g., Search-R1) train against live search engines, which suffer from (1) uncontrolled/unpredictable document quality and (2) prohibitively high API costs over hundreds of thousands of rollout queries. ZeroSearch replaces the live search engine during training with a frozen, lightly SFT-tuned simulation LLM that generates documents, while still using a real engine (Google/SerpAPI) at inference/evaluation. Supervision is outcome-based (rule-based F1 reward on final answer); no step-level supervision.
what_is_retrieved: Documents (passages) in response to a search query. During training these documents are GENERATED by a simulation LLM (5 short docs of ~30 words each per query, controllable as 'useful' or 'noisy'); during inference the policy retrieves real documents from Google Web Search via SerpAPI.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus at inference (real web/Google via SerpAPI; a Wikipedia-compatible variant is also released). During training, retrieval is grounded in a frozen simulation LLM's parametric knowledge that mimics a search engine rather than any external corpus. No agent-written growing/episodic memory.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Fixed top-k ranking style: a fixed k=5 documents are returned per query (both for the simulation LLM and the real engine). The objective is end-to-end answer accuracy (F1 reward / EM eval), not retrieval completeness or a variable-size precision-driven set.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The work does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner; it is an RL-for-search framework.
retrieval_unit: document / passage (short ~30-word documents during simulated training; standard web search snippets/passages at inference). Top-5 documents are concatenated into the <information> block.
index_source: Hybrid by phase. Training-time 'index' is a frozen simulation LLM (offline lightly-SFT-tuned to generate useful vs noisy documents; parametric, not a stored corpus). Inference-time index is a static external corpus = the live web via Google/SerpAPI (or Wikipedia in the released variant). The store is not induced/grown online during deployment.
index_structure_topology: Flat. During training the 'search engine' is a generative LLM (no explicit index structure). During inference a standard flat web-search ranking is used (top-k by the search engine). No graph/hierarchical/cluster topology.
retriever_type: LLM-as-retriever (generative): a fine-tuned simulation LLM generates documents during RL training (the paper's core novelty). At inference, an off-the-shelf real search engine (Google Web Search via SerpAPI) is used. The trained policy model itself is the query generator, not the retriever.
retriever_learning_signal: For the simulation LLM (the 'retriever'): lightweight supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on query-document pairs harvested from real-search interaction trajectories, with an LLM-as-judge labeling each document useful or noisy; document quality is then controlled at rollout by adjusting a few prompt words. The simulation LLM is frozen during RL. The retriever is NOT trained with RL or contrastive similarity labels. (The policy model that issues queries is trained with RL / outcome F1 reward, but it is the agent, not the retriever.)
query_construction: Thought-conditioned, agent-generated free-text search queries. The policy model first reasons inside <think>...</think>, then if it needs evidence emits a query inside <search>...</search>; queries can be reformulated/decomposed across turns (e.g., first search the person, then their birthplace).
query_granularity: Step/turn-level: queries are generated iteratively at each reasoning step during a multi-turn rollout (not a single one-shot query at t=0). Multiple searches per question are allowed (MAX_TURNS=5 in the released code).
when_to_retrieve: Iterative / agent-initiated. The model searches on demand whenever its own reasoning decides external knowledge is needed, across multiple turns, until it chooses to answer.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Agent-initiated request: the policy model itself decides when to emit a <search> query based on its internal reasoning (<think>), with no fixed schedule, confidence threshold, or learned external router. The decision behavior emerges from RL training on the outcome reward.
reranking: None. No explicit reranking stage; the top-5 documents (generated or retrieved) are used directly.
retrieved_context_refinement: None (no rerank, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering of returned documents). Training-time robustness instead comes from deliberately injecting noisy documents via the curriculum, and document tokens are loss-masked during the RL update (not a context-refinement step but a gradient-masking step).
tool_document_engineering: N/A (no tool/skill descriptions are indexed; retrieval target is documents, not tools).
index_content_separation: N/A (no separate lightweight index vs heavy content; documents are generated/retrieved directly).
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A for a tool index. For completeness: inference uses Google Web Search via the SerpAPI HTTP API; training uses a locally served simulation LLM (sglang/vLLM server). No MCP/RapidAPI/function-calling tool registry.
how_retrieved_used: Prompt augmentation: retrieved/generated documents are inserted into the rollout between <information> and </information> tags and conditioned on for the next reasoning step. Retrieval is embedded inside the RL training loop, so the (simulated) retrieved context also indirectly shapes the training signal, but it is not itself a learned latent injection.
planning_integration: Inside a search loop / per-step interleaved retrieve-then-reason. The agent follows a think -> search -> read information -> think -> ... -> answer loop within a single multi-turn rollout (retrieve-as-you-reason), rather than plan-then-retrieve or tree search. Curriculum noise scheduling is applied across training steps, not within a single rollout's plan.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-reasoning-step / per-search-call within a rollout: each <think> step may trigger one <search> call whose returned <information> conditions the next step. Interleaving granularity is at the level of individual search turns, not per-sentence or per-token.
retrieved_item_representation: Raw textual documents (short passages) injected verbatim into the <information> block of the prompt; no distillation into strategies/guidelines or programs.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Raw document/passage (lowest abstraction). No distilled strategy, guideline, workflow, or skill.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Retriever-aware / curriculum training: the simulation LLM can be prompted to emit 'noisy' documents, and a curriculum rollout schedule progressively raises the probability of noisy documents (per the exponential schedule p_i = p_s + (b^{i/m}-1)/(b-1)*(p_e-p_s), default b=4), exposing the policy to increasingly hard/noisy retrieval and forcing it to learn robust reasoning. Document tokens are loss-masked so externally-generated (potentially noisy) tokens do not destabilize the gradient. No explicit relevance evaluator / self-reflection / reason-in-documents module.
memory_type: none (no episodic store, skill library, workflow memory, or graph memory). The only persistent learned artifact is the RL-updated policy weights plus the frozen SFT'd simulation LLM.
write_back: False. The system does not store new experiences/cases/skills into any retrievable memory during deployment; knowledge is internalized in policy weights via RL, not written to an external store.
online_growth: False. No retrievable store grows at test time; the simulation LLM and (inference) search corpus are fixed. Curriculum difficulty changes during training, but that is a schedule, not store growth.
write_back_trigger: never (no write-back to an external memory store; learning is via on-policy RL weight updates rather than memory writes).
failure_experience_usage: No persistent storage/retrieval of failed experiences. Indirectly, 'noisy' (often answer-lacking) documents are deliberately generated during the curriculum to harden the policy, and the outcome-based F1 reward naturally penalizes wrong answers, but failures are not stored as retrievable negative cases.
memory_evolution_update: N/A (no stored memory entries to mutate). The policy is updated by REINFORCE/PPO/GRPO gradient steps.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Partial. The decision of WHEN/WHAT to search is a learned RL policy (the policy model emits search queries, trained with outcome reward). However the retriever/document source itself is NOT a learned/RL retrieval policy: at training it is a frozen SFT'd simulation LLM, and at inference it is a fixed top-k web search engine.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No. Single-agent private training; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. (The paper notes one simulation server could be shared across multiple RL training jobs to cut cost, but that is infrastructure sharing, not experience sharing.)
benchmarks: NQ (Natural Questions), TriviaQA, PopQA (single-hop QA); HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle (multi-hop QA). Training set is the merged NQ + HotpotQA train splits (NQ and HotpotQA are in-domain; the other five are out-of-domain).
benchmark_family: QA: single-hop (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA) and multi-hop (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle).
baselines: Vanilla prompting: Direct Answer, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), standard RAG. Advanced RAG: RAgent (RAG-Agent style iterative search) and Search-o1. RL tuning: R1 (reasoning on internal knowledge only) and Search-R1 (RL with a real search engine). Search-R1 with a real search engine is the primary head-to-head comparison. Ablation comparisons also include prompt-based vs SFT simulation engines (3B/7B/14B) and Google Search itself.
key_metrics: Exact Match (EM) for end-to-end QA accuracy (primary, following Search-R1). F1 score is used as the rule-based RL reward (and as the reward across all RL baselines for fair comparison). Cost metrics: API cost vs GPU cost in USD; reward curves and number of interaction turns are tracked as training dynamics.
headline_result: Using Qwen-2.5-3B-Base as the policy model, ZeroSearch with a fine-tuned 14B simulation engine (SFT-14B) reaches average EM 34.47 across the 7 datasets, surpassing the same policy trained with real Google Search (avg EM 32.81); a fine-tuned 7B simulation engine (SFT-7B, avg 33.53) matches Google. Headline claim: a 7B retrieval module matches a real search engine and a 14B module surpasses it, at zero API cost. Cost: ~64,000 queries cost $70.8 (GPU, SFT-14B) vs $586.7 (Google/SerpAPI API).
ablations: (1) Choice of simulation LLM (Table 4, Qwen-2.5-3B-Base policy): Base-no-RL 8.82 avg; prompt-based Prompt-3B/7B/14B = 29.44/31.39/31.50; SFT-3B/7B/14B = 30.47/33.53/34.47; Google = 32.81 -> SFT engines beat prompt engines, larger is better, SFT-7B ~= Google, SFT-14B > Google. (2) RL algorithm (Table 5): REINFORCE 34.47 > GRPO 33.17 > PPO 32.67 (REINFORCE best/most stable). (3) Curriculum vs random noise=0.5 (Table 6): Curriculum 34.47 vs Random 32.59 on Qwen-2.5-3B-Base; 36.07 vs 34.84 on LLaMA-3.2-3B-Base -> curriculum helps. (4) Document-token loss masking (Table 7, LLaMA-3.2-3B): w/ mask 36.07 vs w/o mask 34.53 -> masking improves stability/performance. (5) Base vs Instruct and reward-curve comparisons vs Search-R1 (Figs 2-4).
evaluation_decoupling: No. Intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / completeness) are not reported separately; evaluation is end-to-end QA EM only. Simulation document quality is shown qualitatively (useful vs noisy case studies) rather than via intrinsic retrieval scores.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Primarily outcome (final-answer EM / F1 reward). Some process-level training-dynamics analysis is reported (reward curves, number of interaction turns over training, base-vs-instruct curves, effect of loss masking), but no formal step-wise retrieval-accuracy or reasoning-faithfulness metric.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Central claim of the paper. For ~64,000 search requests over a ~12h / batch 64 / 5 rollouts / 200-step run: API cost with Google/SerpAPI = $586.7 vs GPU cost for SFT-3B/7B/14B simulation = $17.7 / $35.4 / $70.8 (API cost $0). So ZeroSearch removes API cost entirely at the price of GPU deployment, achieving equal-or-better accuracy than the real engine. REINFORCE/GRPO involve repeated rollouts that would multiply real-engine API cost.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed-k: exactly 5 documents returned per search query for all methods (TOPK=5); MAX_TURNS=5 search turns per question in released code. Simulated documents are short (~30 words each). No adaptive/budget-capped selection or truncation reranking.
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A (not a benchmark paper; uses standard public QA datasets). Evaluation uses 500 examples per dataset (per the reported per-dataset scores following the Search-R1 protocol) [uncertain on exact eval subset size].
builds_on: Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025, arXiv:2503.09516) for the multi-turn think/search/answer RL template, F1-reward choice, dataset setup (NQ+HotpotQA train), and EM evaluation; DeepSeek-R1 / OpenAI-o1 for reward-driven reasoning without step supervision; 'Generate rather than retrieve' (Yu et al., 2022) for the insight that LLMs can generate relevant documents; RL algorithms REINFORCE (Williams 1992), PPO (Schulman et al. 2017), GRPO (DeepSeekMath, Shao et al. 2024). Implementation builds on Search-R1, veRL, and RAGEN codebases.
contrasts_with: Search-R1, R1-Searcher, ReSearch (RL-for-search against static local corpora or real engines), and DeepResearcher / WebThinker (RL with live commercial search engines). ZeroSearch contrasts by simulating the search engine with a frozen SFT'd LLM to remove API cost and gain controllable, curriculum-degraded document quality. Also contrasts with prompt-based / SFT RAG (Self-RAG, RetroLLM, Adaptive-RAG) and MCTS test-time-scaling RAG (RAG-Star, AirRAG, Marco-o1).
lineage: Part of the RL-for-search / agentic-RAG lineage (group B: RAG for task solving). A 2025 sibling of Search-R1 / R1-Searcher / ReSearch / DeepResearcher, distinguished by replacing the live retriever with a simulation LLM during RL training (search-engine simulation for cost-free, quality-controllable RL). Has inspired follow-ups such as SSRL (Self-Search Reinforcement Learning).
